questions.q: A data scientist reports the perplexity of a language model on a held-out corpus. What does perplexity measure?
options: The fraction of next tokens predicted exactly
The average cosine similarity between generated and reference text
The exponentiated average negative log-likelihood per token
The number of distinct tokens the model can generate
questions.why: Perplexity = exp(mean per-token cross-entropy), so it summarizes how well the model's probability distribution predicts held-out text. It is not top-1 next-token accuracy; a model can assign high probability to the right token without it being the argmax every time.

questions.q: Model X has a validation perplexity of 12 and Model Y has 18 on the same dataset with the same tokenizer. Which statement is correct?
options: Model X assigns higher average probability to the validation text
Model Y is better because higher perplexity means more diverse outputs
Model Y has fewer parameters
The two values cannot be compared even with the same tokenizer
questions.why: Lower perplexity means lower average negative log-likelihood, i.e. the model is less "surprised" by the data. With the same data and tokenizer the comparison is valid; higher perplexity does not indicate useful diversity.

questions.q: A model's average negative log-likelihood on a test set is 2.0 nats per token. What is its perplexity, approximately?
questions.why: Perplexity = exp(average NLL) = e^2 ≈ 7.39 when the NLL is measured in nats (natural log). Answering 4.0 would be correct only if the loss were measured in bits (2^2).

questions.q: A language model assigns equal probability to every token in a 50,000-token vocabulary at every position. What is its perplexity?
options: About 10.8
questions.why: If p = 1/V for every token, the NLL per token is ln(V), and exp(ln V) = V. Perplexity can be read as the effective number of equally likely choices; 10.8 is ln(50,000), the loss, not the perplexity.

questions.q: Two teams compare LLMs by perplexity on the same text, but each model uses a different tokenizer. Why is the comparison unreliable?
options: Perplexity is only defined for encoder-only models
Perplexity is normalized per token, and the models split the text into different numbers of tokens
Perplexity depends on the sampling temperature used at inference
Perplexity ignores the first token of every sequence
questions.why: A tokenizer that produces more, smaller tokens spreads the same total log-likelihood over more units, changing per-token perplexity. Tokenizer-independent measures such as bits per byte or per character fix this; temperature does not affect perplexity, which is computed from the model's raw probabilities.

questions.q: Which description best matches the BLEU metric used in machine translation?
options: Modified n-gram precision against references, combined with a brevity penalty
Recall of reference unigrams in the candidate
Cosine similarity of contextual embeddings
Character n-gram F-score
questions.why: BLEU takes the geometric mean of clipped 1- to 4-gram precisions and multiplies it by a brevity penalty for short outputs. Recall-oriented overlap is the core idea of ROUGE, and character n-gram F-score describes chrF.

questions.q: A developer is evaluating an LLM-based news summarizer against human-written reference summaries. Which metric family is most traditionally used for this?
options: BLEU
Perplexity
ROUGE
pass@k
questions.why: ROUGE (Recall-Oriented Understudy for Gisting Evaluation) was designed for summarization and emphasizes how much of the reference content appears in the candidate. BLEU was designed for translation and is precision-oriented.

questions.q: What does ROUGE-L measure?
options: Overlap of bigrams between candidate and reference
The longest common subsequence between candidate and reference
The length ratio between candidate and reference
Overlap of synonyms using WordNet
questions.why: ROUGE-L uses the longest common subsequence, which rewards in-order matches without requiring them to be contiguous. Bigram overlap is ROUGE-2.

questions.q: A reference summary has 12 unigrams. The candidate summary has 10 unigrams, 9 of which also appear in the reference. What is ROUGE-1 recall?
questions.why: ROUGE-1 recall = overlapping unigrams / unigrams in the reference = 9/12 = 0.75. The value 0.90 (9/10) is ROUGE-1 precision, which divides by the candidate length, and 0.82 is their F1.

questions.q: On an extractive QA benchmark, the gold answer is "Abraham Lincoln" and the model outputs "President Abraham Lincoln". Under SQuAD-style normalization, what is the exact match (EM) score for this item?
questions.why: Exact match gives credit only if the normalized prediction equals the normalized gold string; normalization removes case, punctuation and articles, but not the extra word "President". Token-level F1 would give partial credit (0.8) here.

questions.q: Gold answer: "the eiffel tower in paris". Prediction: "eiffel tower". After SQuAD normalization (articles removed), what is token-level F1?
questions.why: After removing "the", the gold tokens are {eiffel, tower, in, paris} (4) and the prediction tokens are {eiffel, tower} (2). Precision = 2/2 = 1.0 and recall = 2/4 = 0.5, so F1 = 2·1·0.5/(1+0.5) ≈ 0.67. The value 0.40 would come from wrongly counting "the" in the gold answer and using recall only (2/5).

questions.q: A team reports HumanEval pass@1 and pass@10 for a code LLM. What does pass@k represent?
options: The fraction of unit tests passed across all problems
The probability that at least one of k generated samples passes all unit tests
The BLEU score of the best of k samples
The number of attempts needed before the first passing solution
questions.why: pass@k is a functional-correctness metric: a problem counts as solved if any of k sampled programs passes its hidden tests. It does not award partial credit for passing some tests, and it does not use text-similarity metrics like BLEU.

questions.q: Why is pass@k generally preferred over BLEU for evaluating code generation?
options: BLEU cannot be computed on programming languages
pass@k is cheaper to compute than BLEU
Syntactically different programs can be functionally equivalent, and similar-looking code can be wrong
BLEU only works when there are multiple references
questions.why: Executing code against unit tests checks behavior directly, whereas n-gram overlap rewards surface similarity. BLEU can technically be computed on code tokens; it simply correlates poorly with correctness, and pass@k is actually more expensive because it requires sandboxed execution.

questions.q: What does the MMLU benchmark primarily measure?
options: Multi-turn conversational quality judged by GPT-4
Commonsense sentence completion
Grade-school math word problems
Broad knowledge and reasoning via multiple-choice questions across 57 subjects
questions.why: MMLU (Massive Multitask Language Understanding) covers 57 subjects such as STEM, law and humanities with four-choice questions. Commonsense sentence completion describes HellaSwag, and grade-school math describes GSM8K.

questions.q: Which benchmark tests commonsense reasoning by asking a model to choose the most plausible continuation of a scenario, with wrong endings produced by adversarial filtering?
options: HellaSwag
ARC
TruthfulQA
GSM8K
questions.why: HellaSwag presents a context and four candidate endings; the distractors were machine-generated and adversarially filtered so they fool models while being easy for humans. ARC is a grade-school science multiple-choice benchmark, not a continuation task.

questions.q: A researcher wants to measure multi-step arithmetic reasoning on natural-language word problems. Which benchmark is the best fit?
options: MMLU
GSM8K
HumanEval
HellaSwag
questions.why: GSM8K contains about 8.5K grade-school math word problems that require several arithmetic steps, and answers are checked against a final numeric value. MMLU includes some math subjects but is broad multiple-choice knowledge rather than step-by-step problem solving.

questions.q: What is HumanEval?
options: A crowdsourced platform where humans vote between two chatbots
A set of human-written summaries for ROUGE evaluation
A set of hand-written Python programming problems with unit tests
A human-preference dataset for RLHF reward models
questions.why: HumanEval (from OpenAI's Codex paper) has 164 Python problems, each with a function signature, docstring and hidden unit tests, and is scored with pass@k. The crowdsourced voting platform is Chatbot Arena.

questions.q: Which benchmark is specifically designed to test whether a model repeats common human misconceptions instead of giving true answers?
options: BIG-bench
ARC-Challenge
MT-Bench
TruthfulQA
questions.why: TruthfulQA contains questions where popular misconceptions make a false answer tempting ("imitative falsehoods"). Notably, larger models trained to imitate web text can score worse on it, which is why it is used to probe truthfulness rather than knowledge breadth.

questions.q: How does Chatbot Arena rank LLMs?
options: By crowdsourced pairwise human votes between anonymous models, aggregated into Elo-style ratings
By averaging MMLU and GSM8K accuracy
By GPT-4 scoring single answers on a 1–10 scale
By measuring tokens per second on identical hardware
questions.why: Users chat with two anonymous models side by side and vote for the better response; votes are aggregated into Elo / Bradley–Terry ratings. GPT-4 grading answers on a 1–10 scale describes MT-Bench's single-answer grading mode.

questions.q: What distinguishes MT-Bench from single-turn knowledge benchmarks?
options: It uses only code-execution tests
It evaluates multi-turn conversations, typically scored by a strong LLM acting as a judge
It measures translation quality with BLEU
It contains over 100,000 crowdsourced questions
questions.why: MT-Bench has 80 two-turn questions across categories such as writing, reasoning, math and coding, and is graded by an LLM judge (originally GPT-4). It is intentionally small; the large crowdsourced dataset is Chatbot Arena's vote log.

questions.q: A model scores unusually high on a public benchmark, and the team discovers the benchmark's test questions were present in the pretraining crawl. What is this problem called?
options: Overfitting to the validation set
Distribution shift
Benchmark (data) contamination
Catastrophic forgetting
questions.why: Contamination means test items leaked into training data, so the score reflects memorization rather than generalization. Distribution shift is the opposite situation: test data differs from what the model saw.

questions.q: What is the "LLM-as-a-judge" evaluation approach?
options: Fine-tuning an LLM on legal documents
Using an LLM to generate the test set's reference answers only
Using human judges to label LLM outputs
Using a strong LLM, guided by a prompt or rubric, to score or compare model outputs
questions.why: LLM-as-a-judge replaces or supplements human raters with a capable model that grades responses pointwise or compares them pairwise. It scales cheaply for open-ended outputs where n-gram metrics fail, but it must be validated against human judgments because judges have biases.

questions.q: A team wants to measure whether a chat model obeys explicit constraints such as "answer in exactly three bullet points" or "do not use commas." Which benchmark is designed for this?
options: IFEval
HellaSwag
TruthfulQA
GSM8K
questions.why: IFEval uses instructions whose compliance can be checked programmatically (word counts, formats, forbidden characters), so no human or LLM judge is needed. TruthfulQA measures whether a model repeats common misconceptions, not whether it follows formatting constraints.

questions.q: An LLM judge consistently rates longer answers higher even when the extra text adds no correct information. What is the most direct name for this?
options: Position bias
Recency bias
Verbosity (length) bias
Self-preference bias
questions.why: Verbosity bias makes judges favor longer, more detailed-looking outputs. It is mitigated with rubrics that penalize padding, reference answers, or length-controlled win rates; it has nothing to do with the order responses appear in.

questions.q: A team uses Model M as a judge to compare Model M's outputs against a competitor's outputs. What risk is most specific to this setup?
options: The judge will run out of context window
The judge may favor outputs resembling its own style (self-preference bias)
The judge cannot read outputs from other models
The judge's scores become deterministic
questions.why: LLM judges have been shown to rate their own or same-family outputs more favorably. Using a different judge model, a panel of judges, or validating against human labels reduces this risk.

questions.q: When is human evaluation most valuable compared to automatic metrics?
options: When outputs are open-ended and qualities like helpfulness, tone or factual nuance matter
When the task has a single exact answer that can be string-matched
When thousands of evaluations are needed every hour in CI
When measuring tokens-per-second throughput
questions.why: Humans can judge subjective and nuanced qualities that overlap metrics miss, which is why human evaluation remains the reference standard for open-ended generation. For exact-answer tasks or high-volume CI checks, automatic metrics are cheaper and sufficient.

questions.q: Why do evaluation teams report inter-annotator agreement for human ratings?
options: To compute the model's perplexity
To check whether the rating task is well defined and the labels are consistent across raters
To reduce the number of annotators needed to one
To measure how fast annotators work
questions.why: Low agreement signals ambiguous guidelines or a subjective task, which limits how much any model score built on those labels can be trusted. It also sets a practical ceiling: a model cannot meaningfully "agree with humans" more than humans agree with each other.

questions.q: What advantage does Cohen's kappa have over raw percent agreement between two annotators?
options: It works with any number of annotators
It is always higher than percent agreement
It measures annotator speed
It corrects for the agreement expected by chance
questions.why: κ = (p_o − p_e)/(1 − p_e), subtracting the chance agreement p_e implied by each rater's label frequencies. Cohen's kappa is defined for two raters; Fleiss' kappa or Krippendorff's alpha handle more.

questions.q: What is a "golden dataset" in LLM application evaluation?
options: The full pretraining corpus of the model
A set of synthetic prompts generated on the fly for each run
A curated, versioned set of inputs with trusted expected outputs or criteria used as a fixed reference
The data with the highest loss during training
questions.why: A golden set is a stable, high-quality reference so results are comparable across model, prompt and pipeline versions. Regenerating prompts on every run would defeat that comparability.

questions.q: Which pairing correctly contrasts offline and online evaluation?
options: Offline uses real users; online uses fixed test sets
Offline uses fixed datasets before deployment; online measures behavior with real traffic after deployment
Offline is only for classification; online is only for generation
Offline requires GPUs; online does not
questions.why: Offline evaluation runs benchmarks or golden sets in a controlled setting; online evaluation (A/B tests, user feedback, production monitoring) captures real usage. The two complement each other because offline gains do not always translate to user-facing improvements.

questions.q: What is the purpose of an A/B test when deploying a new LLM prompt?
options: To randomly split live traffic between the old and new variants and compare outcome metrics
To test the prompt on two different GPUs
To compare the prompt's BLEU against its ROUGE
To evaluate the prompt on the training set and the test set
questions.why: Randomized assignment makes the groups comparable, so differences in outcomes (e.g., resolution rate, thumbs-up rate) can be attributed to the variant. Comparing train vs test performance is a generalization check, not an A/B test.

questions.q: An A/B test reports p = 0.03 for the difference in user satisfaction. What does this mean?
options: There is a 3% probability that the new variant is better
The effect size is 3%
If there were truly no difference, data at least this extreme would occur about 3% of the time
97% of users preferred the new variant
questions.why: A p-value is computed assuming the null hypothesis is true; it is not the probability that the hypothesis is true or false. It also says nothing about how large the effect is.

questions.q: Which practice most directly improves the reproducibility of an LLM fine-tuning experiment?
options: Using the largest batch size the GPU allows
Evaluating only on the training set
Running each experiment exactly once
Fixing random seeds and recording code, data, config and model versions
questions.why: Reproducibility means someone can rerun the experiment and obtain the same (or statistically consistent) results, which requires controlling randomness and versioning every input. Batch size choice affects results but does not make them reproducible by itself.

questions.q: A team wants to log hyperparameters, metrics, artifacts and model versions for every training run and compare runs in a UI. Which tools fit this need?
options: MLflow or Weights & Biases
TensorRT-LLM or Triton Inference Server
NeMo Guardrails or Presidio
cuDF or cuML
questions.why: MLflow and W&B are experiment-tracking platforms that record parameters, metrics and artifacts and provide run comparison dashboards (and model registries). TensorRT-LLM and Triton are inference optimization and serving tools, not trackers.

questions.q: A researcher removes the retrieval re-ranker from a pipeline, keeps everything else fixed, and measures the drop in answer accuracy. What kind of experiment is this?
options: Hyperparameter sweep
Ablation study
A/B test
Cross-validation
questions.why: An ablation removes or disables one component while holding others constant to measure that component's contribution. A hyperparameter sweep varies settings of a fixed design rather than removing parts of it.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes random search compared with grid search for hyperparameter tuning?
options: Random search always finds the global optimum
Grid search scales better as the number of hyperparameters grows
Random search samples configurations from distributions and often finds good settings with fewer trials when only a few hyperparameters matter
Random search requires a surrogate model of the objective
questions.why: Grid search wastes trials repeating the same values of important parameters while varying unimportant ones; random search explores more distinct values of each dimension. A surrogate model is the defining feature of Bayesian optimization, not random search.

questions.q: What distinguishes Bayesian optimization from grid and random search?
options: It evaluates all combinations exhaustively
It requires gradients of the validation metric
It only tunes the learning rate
It builds a surrogate model of the objective and uses an acquisition function to choose the next trial
questions.why: Bayesian optimization (e.g., Gaussian processes or TPE as in Optuna) uses past trial results to predict promising regions and balances exploration and exploitation via acquisition functions like expected improvement. It is gradient-free; gradient-based hyperparameter optimization is a separate family.

questions.q: An ML engineer wants to check whether a new automatic summary-quality metric ranks outputs the same way human raters do. Which statistic is most appropriate?
options: Spearman rank correlation between metric scores and human ratings
Cohen's kappa between the metric and one human rater
Perplexity of the summaries under the evaluated model
Mean squared error between metric scores and summary lengths
questions.why: A rank correlation (Spearman or Kendall's tau) measures whether the metric orders outputs the way humans do, even when the two use different scales. Cohen's kappa measures agreement on categorical labels, not continuous scores on different scales.

questions.q: Both training and validation loss plateau at a high value early and stay close together. What is the most likely issue?
options: Overfitting
Underfitting (insufficient capacity, too few steps, or too low a learning rate)
Benchmark contamination
Test-set leakage
questions.why: When the model cannot even fit the training data well, both curves stay high with little gap — the signature of underfitting. Overfitting requires training loss to be noticeably lower than validation loss.

questions.q: In 100 pairwise comparisons against a baseline, model A wins 55, loses 25 and ties 20. Counting each tie as half a win, what is model A's win rate?
questions.why: Win rate = (55 + 0.5 × 20) / 100 = 0.65. 0.55 ignores ties entirely, and 0.69 (55/80) drops ties from the denominator, which is a different convention from the one requested.

questions.q: What is the correct role of the test set in a model development workflow?
options: To tune hyperparameters after each epoch
To select the best checkpoint during training
To provide additional training examples when data is scarce
To give a final, unbiased estimate of performance after all model choices are made
questions.why: Hyperparameter tuning and checkpoint selection belong to the validation set. Using the test set for those decisions leaks information and makes the final number optimistically biased.

questions.q: A team randomly splits a customer-support dataset and finds many near-duplicate tickets appear in both training and test sets. What is the main consequence?
options: Test scores will be inflated and overestimate real-world performance
Training will take longer
The model will underfit
Test scores will be artificially low
questions.why: Near-duplicates across splits let the model succeed by recall of seen examples, a form of leakage. Deduplicating before splitting (or splitting by customer, time or template) gives a more honest estimate.

questions.q: What does it mean for an LLM classifier to be well calibrated?
options: It has the highest possible accuracy
Its predicted confidence matches its empirical accuracy (e.g., 80%-confidence predictions are right about 80% of the time)
It always outputs probabilities near 0 or 1
Its loss is identical on training and validation sets
questions.why: Calibration concerns the reliability of probabilities, not accuracy itself; a model can be accurate but overconfident. Pushing probabilities to the extremes typically worsens calibration when the model is not actually that certain.

questions.q: How is Expected Calibration Error (ECE) computed?
options: The average cross-entropy over the test set
The maximum gap between confidence and accuracy over all samples
The fraction of predictions above 0.5 confidence
A weighted average, over confidence bins, of the absolute gap between average confidence and accuracy
questions.why: ECE bins predictions by confidence and averages |accuracy − confidence| weighted by the number of samples per bin. The maximum per-bin gap is a different metric, Maximum Calibration Error (MCE).

questions.q: A support chatbot scores 92% accuracy on the overall test set, yet Spanish-speaking customers report frequent wrong answers. Which evaluation practice would have revealed this before launch?
options: Reporting metrics per data slice, such as language or customer segment
Increasing the overall test set size
Switching the metric from accuracy to perplexity
Running more trials of hyperparameter search
questions.why: Aggregate metrics can hide poor performance on small subgroups; breaking results down by slice shows exactly where the model fails. A larger test set with the same mix would still be dominated by the majority slice and give a similar headline number.

questions.q: A summarization model sometimes adds facts that are not in the source document. Which evaluation dimension directly targets this problem?
options: Fluency
Perplexity on the source
Faithfulness (factual consistency with the source)
ROUGE-2 recall
questions.why: Faithfulness checks whether every claim in the output is supported by the input; unsupported additions are hallucinations. ROUGE-2 recall measures how much reference content is covered and can stay high even when invented facts are added.

questions.q: Which feature distinguishes METEOR from BLEU?
options: It counts only 4-gram matches
It matches stems and synonyms in addition to exact words and weights recall more heavily
It uses contextual embeddings from BERT
It requires executing the output
questions.why: METEOR aligns unigrams using exact, stem and synonym (WordNet) matches, computes a recall-weighted harmonic mean, and applies a fragmentation penalty for word order. Contextual embeddings describe BERTScore.

questions.q: A team wants a reference-based metric that gives credit for paraphrases like "car" vs "automobile". Which metric is best suited?
options: BLEU
Exact match
ROUGE-1
BERTScore
questions.why: BERTScore matches tokens via cosine similarity of contextual embeddings, so semantically equivalent words get high similarity. BLEU, ROUGE-1 and exact match all require surface-form overlap.

questions.q: For translation into a morphologically rich language like Finnish, which metric is often more robust than word-level BLEU?
options: chrF
Perplexity
pass@k
Exact match
questions.why: chrF computes an F-score over character n-grams, so partially matching word forms (different inflections of the same stem) still earn credit. Word-level BLEU treats each inflected form as a complete mismatch.

questions.q: After each prompt or model change, a team automatically reruns a fixed set of evaluation cases and blocks the release if key scores drop. What is this practice called?
options: Online A/B testing
Hyperparameter search
Regression testing on an evaluation suite
Red teaming
questions.why: An evaluation regression suite in CI catches quality drops before release, the LLM analogue of software regression tests. A/B testing happens with live users after deployment, not as a pre-release gate.

questions.q: An LLM classifier flags fraudulent support messages. Only 2% of messages are fraudulent, and the model reaches 98% accuracy. What is the most likely issue?
options: The model may be predicting "not fraud" for everything; accuracy is misleading on imbalanced data
98% accuracy guarantees strong fraud detection
The model is overfitting the minority class
Accuracy cannot be computed for LLM classifiers
questions.why: A trivial majority-class predictor already achieves 98% accuracy here. Per-class metrics such as recall on the fraud class (or a confusion matrix) reveal whether the model actually catches fraud.

questions.q: A team wants to run standard academic benchmarks such as MMLU, HellaSwag and ARC on a Hugging Face model with consistent prompts and scoring. Which open-source tool is designed for this?
options: TensorRT-LLM
EleutherAI lm-evaluation-harness
NeMo Guardrails
Apache Spark
questions.why: lm-evaluation-harness implements hundreds of benchmark tasks with standardized few-shot prompting and scoring, which is why it backs many public leaderboards. TensorRT-LLM optimizes inference; it does not define benchmarks.

questions.q: For one problem, a team samples n = 10 programs and c = 2 pass the tests. Using the unbiased estimator pass@k = 1 − C(n−c, k)/C(n, k), what is pass@5 for this problem?
options: About 0.78
questions.why: C(8,5) = 56 and C(10,5) = 252, so pass@5 = 1 − 56/252 ≈ 1 − 0.222 = 0.778. The value 0.20 is pass@1 (c/n), which is much lower because a single draw has fewer chances to hit a correct program.

questions.q: A model generates 20 samples per problem at temperature 0.8. On one problem, 5 samples pass. What is the unbiased pass@1 estimate for that problem?
questions.why: With k = 1 the unbiased estimator reduces to c/n = 5/20 = 0.25, the probability that one random sample is correct. The benchmark-level pass@1 is the average of this per-problem value across all problems.

questions.q: A translation system outputs very short sentences containing only words it is sure about, giving near-perfect n-gram precision. How does BLEU handle this?
options: It rewards the short outputs with a higher score
It applies a brevity penalty when the candidate is shorter than the reference
It switches to recall-based scoring automatically
It ignores outputs shorter than four tokens
questions.why: Because BLEU is precision-based, it would otherwise reward terse outputs; the brevity penalty BP = exp(1 − r/c) for c < r scales the score down. BLEU never switches to recall — the brevity penalty is its substitute for a recall term.

questions.q: A developer computes BLEU on a single short sentence and gets 0.0 even though most words match the reference. What is the most likely reason?
options: There is no matching 4-gram, so the geometric mean of n-gram precisions collapses to zero without smoothing
The brevity penalty always equals zero for single sentences
BLEU cannot handle lowercase text
The reference had synonyms the candidate missed
questions.why: BLEU multiplies the 1- to 4-gram precisions, so a single zero precision zeroes the whole score. Smoothing methods or corpus-level BLEU avoid this; the brevity penalty is at most a reduction factor and is never exactly zero.

questions.q: Two papers report BLEU on the same test set but used different tokenization and normalization. What tool was created to make such BLEU scores comparable and reproducible?
options: ROUGE-L
BERTScore
COMET
SacreBLEU
questions.why: BLEU varies substantially with preprocessing; SacreBLEU fixes the tokenization and reports a signature string describing the exact settings. COMET is a learned translation metric, not a standardization of BLEU.

questions.q: Two annotators labeling responses as acceptable/unacceptable agree on 80% of items. Based on their label frequencies, chance agreement would be 50%. What is Cohen's kappa?
questions.why: κ = (p_o − p_e)/(1 − p_e) = (0.80 − 0.50)/(1 − 0.50) = 0.60, usually read as moderate-to-substantial agreement. Reporting 0.30 forgets to divide by the maximum achievable improvement over chance (1 − p_e).

questions.q: Five annotators each rate a subset of responses on a 1–5 ordinal scale, and not every annotator rates every item. Which agreement statistic is most appropriate?
options: Krippendorff's alpha
Cohen's kappa
Pearson correlation between two raters
Raw percent agreement
questions.why: Krippendorff's alpha supports any number of raters, missing ratings and ordinal (or interval) data. Cohen's kappa is defined for exactly two raters rating the same items with nominal labels.

questions.q: An ML engineer uses an LLM judge for pairwise comparisons. What is the standard mitigation for position bias?
options: Always put the baseline response first
Use a longer judge prompt
Evaluate each pair in both orders and only count consistent verdicts (or treat inconsistency as a tie)
Increase the judge's temperature
questions.why: Swapping positions and requiring agreement cancels out a preference for slot A or B. Fixing the baseline in the first slot keeps the bias constant but systematically skews every comparison in one direction.

questions.q: A team needs to choose between two closely matched prompt variants. Why might pairwise LLM judging be preferred over pointwise 1–10 scoring?
options: Pairwise judging requires no prompt
Pairwise judging is immune to all judge biases
Pointwise scores cannot be averaged
Relative comparisons are usually more consistent than absolute scores for detecting small quality differences
questions.why: Judges (human or LLM) find "which is better?" easier and more stable than assigning calibrated absolute scores, which tend to cluster. Pairwise judging still suffers from position and verbosity bias, and it scales poorly if you need absolute tracking across many versions.

questions.q: An LLM judge gives inconsistent 1–5 helpfulness scores across reruns. Which change to the judging prompt is most likely to help?
options: Define each score level with concrete, observable criteria and examples
Ask the judge to output only a number with no criteria
Expand the scale to 1–100 for more resolution
Remove the user question from the judge prompt
questions.why: Anchored rubrics reduce ambiguity about what distinguishes a 3 from a 4, increasing consistency. A finer 1–100 scale adds false precision and usually increases variance rather than reducing it.

questions.q: Before relying on an LLM judge for release decisions, what should a team do first?
options: Confirm the judge model is larger than the model being evaluated
Measure the judge's agreement with human labels on a representative sample
Run the judge once at temperature 1.0
Use the judge to also generate the reference answers
questions.why: A judge is only useful if its verdicts track human judgment for your task, which must be measured (e.g., agreement rate or kappa against human labels). Model size alone does not guarantee alignment with your criteria.

questions.q: Which method is commonly used to check whether benchmark test items appear in a model's training corpus?
options: Comparing BLEU and ROUGE scores on the benchmark
Measuring inference latency on benchmark items
Searching for long n-gram overlaps between benchmark items and training documents
Increasing the number of few-shot examples
questions.why: Long n-gram overlap (e.g., the 13-gram check used in the GPT-3 paper) flags test items that appeared verbatim in training data. Changing few-shot count affects scores but says nothing about whether data leaked.

questions.q: Some benchmarks such as BIG-bench embed a unique "canary" GUID string in their files. What is it for?
options: To let model developers filter the benchmark out of training data and detect if a model has memorized it
To encrypt the answer keys
To speed up evaluation by caching results
To track which users downloaded the benchmark
questions.why: Crawlers can exclude any document containing the canary, and if a model can reproduce the canary string, that is evidence the benchmark leaked into training. It does not encrypt anything; the data remain in plain text.

questions.q: Which description fits BIG-bench?
options: A single math benchmark with 8.5K problems
A leaderboard of human pairwise votes
A Python coding benchmark with unit tests
A large collaborative suite of 200+ diverse tasks intended to probe capabilities beyond standard benchmarks
questions.why: BIG-bench (Beyond the Imitation Game) was contributed by hundreds of researchers and spans reasoning, linguistics, social bias and more; BIG-Bench Hard is a 23-task subset where models initially lagged humans. The 8.5K-problem math set is GSM8K.

questions.q: What does the "Challenge" set in the AI2 Reasoning Challenge (ARC) contain?
options: Adversarially generated sentence endings
Grade-school science multiple-choice questions that simple retrieval and co-occurrence baselines answer incorrectly
Competitive programming problems
Questions about common misconceptions
questions.why: ARC splits its science questions into Easy and Challenge, where Challenge items were those that retrieval-based and word co-occurrence baselines failed. Adversarially generated endings describe HellaSwag.

questions.q: A small model scores 26% on MMLU. How should this be interpreted?
options: It is roughly at random-guess level, since each question has four options
It shows strong knowledge in about a quarter of subjects
It indicates benchmark contamination
It is a good score for a model of any size
questions.why: With four choices, random guessing yields about 25%, so 26% shows essentially no measurable MMLU ability. Always compare benchmark scores against the chance baseline before interpreting them.

questions.q: In an Elo system, model A is rated 400 points above model B. Using E_A = 1/(1 + 10^((R_B − R_A)/400)), what is A's expected win probability against B?
options: About 0.50
About 0.76
About 0.91
About 0.99
questions.why: E_A = 1/(1 + 10^(−1)) = 1/1.1 ≈ 0.909. A 200-point gap would give about 0.76, which is a common confusion.

questions.q: An A/B test needs about 4,000 users per arm to detect a 2-percentage-point improvement in task success. Holding power and significance level fixed, roughly how many users per arm are needed to detect a 1-point improvement?
options: About 2,000
About 8,000
About 4,000
About 16,000
questions.why: Required sample size scales with 1/δ², so halving the minimum detectable effect multiplies the needed sample by four. Doubling (8,000) is the common mistake of assuming a linear relationship.

questions.q: A team compares two chatbot variants on 20 independent metrics, each tested at α = 0.05, and finds one significant difference. What is the best interpretation?
options: The variant is definitely better on that metric
About one false positive is expected among 20 tests by chance, so the result needs correction or confirmation
The test lacked power on the other 19 metrics only
α should be raised to 0.10 to find more differences
questions.why: With 20 tests at α = 0.05, the expected number of false positives under the null is 1. A Bonferroni correction (α/20 = 0.0025), a pre-registered primary metric, or a confirmation test is needed before acting on it.

questions.q: A product manager checks an A/B test's p-value every day and stops as soon as it drops below 0.05. What is the problem?
options: Repeated peeking with early stopping inflates the false-positive rate well above 5%
p-values can only be computed once per week
It reduces the statistical power to zero
It makes the confidence interval wider than necessary
questions.why: Each look is another chance for random fluctuation to cross the threshold, so the overall Type I error rate grows with the number of peeks. Use a fixed pre-computed sample size or a sequential testing method designed for continuous monitoring.

questions.q: A golden-set evaluation of 400 items shows 80% accuracy. What is the approximate 95% confidence interval using the normal approximation?
questions.why: SE = √(0.8·0.2/400) = √0.0004 = 0.02, and 1.96 × 0.02 ≈ 0.039, giving about 76.1%–83.9%. The 78%–82% option uses ±1 standard error, which is only about a 68% interval.

questions.q: With 2 million users per arm, an A/B test finds a statistically significant 0.05% increase in thumbs-up rate but the new model doubles serving cost. What should the team conclude?
options: Ship it, because the result is statistically significant
Rerun the test with fewer users
The p-value must be wrong
The effect is real but likely too small to justify the cost; practical significance matters
questions.why: Huge samples make tiny effects statistically significant; the decision should weigh effect size against costs and guardrail metrics. Statistical significance only says the difference is unlikely to be zero, not that it is worth shipping.

questions.q: An A/B test was configured for a 50/50 split, but the logs show 52,000 users in control and 48,000 in treatment. What should the team do first?
options: Proceed with the analysis, since the difference is small
Investigate the assignment or logging pipeline for a sample ratio mismatch before trusting results
Discard 4,000 control users at random
Switch to a one-sided test
questions.why: With 100,000 users, a 52/48 split is extremely unlikely under true 50/50 randomization, indicating a bug (e.g., treatment crashes dropping users from logs) that can bias outcome metrics. Randomly discarding users does not remove the underlying bias.

questions.q: A new chatbot UI shows a large engagement lift in its first three days, which then fades over two weeks. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Benchmark contamination
Sample ratio mismatch
A novelty effect; tests should run long enough to observe steady-state behavior
Regression to the training distribution
questions.why: Users often engage more with anything new, inflating early results. Running tests across full weekly cycles and examining the effect over time helps separate novelty from durable improvement.

questions.q: In an A/B test of a new LLM, the primary metric is answer helpfulness. Which metrics are best treated as guardrail metrics that must not regress?
options: p95 latency, cost per request and safety-violation rate
Training loss and gradient norm
Number of model parameters
BLEU on the pretraining corpus
questions.why: Guardrail metrics protect user experience and business constraints while the primary metric is optimized. Training loss and gradient norms are development diagnostics, not live-traffic outcomes.

questions.q: A self-hosted model runs on a GPU instance costing $4.00 per hour and sustains 2,000 output tokens per second at full utilization. What is the approximate cost per one million output tokens?
questions.why: 2,000 tok/s × 3,600 s = 7.2M tokens per hour, so $4.00 / 7.2 ≈ $0.56 per million tokens. This assumes full utilization; real costs rise when the GPU sits partly idle.

questions.q: An engineer increases the inference batch size on Triton. Aggregate tokens/second rises sharply, but users complain responses feel slower. What explains this?
options: Larger batches reduce model accuracy
Batching disables streaming
Throughput and latency are the same metric measured differently
Larger batches improve GPU utilization and throughput but can increase per-request latency
questions.why: Batching amortizes weight loading across more requests, raising total throughput, but each request may wait in the queue or decode more slowly per step. Evaluation should report both dimensions, ideally as a throughput-versus-latency curve.

questions.q: Why do LLM serving SLOs usually specify p95 or p99 latency instead of mean latency?
options: The mean is always larger than p99
Tail percentiles capture the slow experiences a meaningful fraction of users actually hit, which the mean can hide
Percentiles are easier to compute than means
Mean latency cannot be measured for streaming responses
questions.why: Latency distributions for LLMs are skewed by long prompts and long outputs, so a good mean can coexist with many very slow requests. p95/p99 targets make sure that tail is controlled.

questions.q: Several frontier models all score above 90% on a popular benchmark, and the gaps between them are within run-to-run noise. What should a team choosing among these models do?
options: Treat the benchmark as saturated and compare on harder or task-specific evaluations
Pick the model with the highest score, since any gap is meaningful
Re-run the same benchmark with more seeds until a clear winner appears
Average the benchmark score with perplexity to break ties
questions.why: When top scores cluster near the ceiling, where label noise also lives, the benchmark no longer discriminates between models; harder successors or the team's own task evals are more informative. More seeds reduce noise but cannot create headroom the benchmark lacks.

questions.q: Throughout training, validation loss is slightly lower than training loss. Which explanation is most plausible?
options: The model is severely overfitting
Regularization such as dropout is active during training but disabled during evaluation
The learning rate is too low
The validation set is larger than the training set
questions.why: Dropout makes training-mode forward passes noisier, and training loss is often averaged over an epoch while the model was still improving. Overfitting would push validation loss above training loss, not below it (though an unexpectedly large gap is worth checking for leakage or an easier validation set).

questions.q: Fine-tuning run A beats run B by 0.6 accuracy points on a 500-item test set, each from a single seed. What should the team do before claiming A is better?
options: Report A's best checkpoint only
Increase A's learning rate and compare again
Repeat both runs over several seeds and compare mean ± standard deviation
Evaluate both on the training set
questions.why: Seed-to-seed variance in fine-tuning can easily exceed 0.6 points, so a single run cannot separate signal from noise. Reporting the distribution across seeds (or a significance test) is the reproducible way to compare.

questions.q: A team fixes all random seeds but still sees tiny differences between two identical training runs on GPUs. What is the most likely cause?
options: The seeds were not saved in the config file
Python's garbage collector
The tokenizer randomly changes its vocabulary
Nondeterministic GPU kernels, such as atomic floating-point additions whose order varies
questions.why: Floating-point addition is not associative, so parallel reductions in different orders produce slightly different results. Frameworks offer deterministic modes (e.g., `torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True)`), usually at some speed cost.

questions.q: To make benchmark scores for a chat model as repeatable as possible across runs, which decoding setting is most appropriate?
options: Greedy decoding (temperature 0) with fixed max tokens and stop sequences
Temperature 1.2 with top-p 0.95
A different random seed for every item
Beam search with a random beam width
questions.why: Greedy decoding removes sampling randomness, so variation comes only from numerical effects. High-temperature sampling adds variance that would require many repetitions to estimate reliably.

questions.q: A team's evaluation scores changed after a teammate edited the system prompt in production, but nobody can tell which prompt produced which result. What practice would have prevented this?
options: Using a larger evaluation set
Running evaluations only on weekends
Versioning prompts alongside code, data and model, and logging the prompt version with each evaluation run
Switching from ROUGE to BLEU
questions.why: In LLM applications, the prompt is a first-class artifact that changes behavior as much as weights do. Tracking it in version control and attaching its version to every run makes results attributable and reproducible.

questions.q: Which MLflow component manages model versions and lifecycle stages (e.g., staging, production) for deployment governance?
options: MLflow Tracking
MLflow Projects
MLflow Recipes
MLflow Model Registry
questions.why: The Model Registry stores versioned models with lineage to the runs that produced them and supports stage transitions and aliases. MLflow Tracking logs parameters and metrics per run but does not manage promotion of model versions.

questions.q: When sampling learning rates for random search between 1e-6 and 1e-3, how should the values be drawn?
options: Uniformly on a linear scale
Log-uniformly, so each order of magnitude is equally likely
Only at the two endpoints
From a normal distribution centered at 5e-4
questions.why: Learning-rate effects are roughly multiplicative, so a linear-uniform draw would put about 90% of samples between 1e-4 and 1e-3 and barely explore smaller values. Log-uniform sampling spreads trials evenly across 1e-6, 1e-5, 1e-4 and 1e-3 decades.

questions.q: A hyperparameter search with 100 fine-tuning trials is too expensive. Which approach reduces cost by terminating unpromising trials early based on intermediate validation scores?
options: Grid search
Successive halving methods such as Hyperband or ASHA
Increasing the number of epochs per trial
K-fold cross-validation
questions.why: These schedulers give many trials a small budget, then repeatedly promote only the best fraction to larger budgets. Cross-validation increases the cost per trial rather than reducing it.

questions.q:
A RAG pipeline ablation gives these answer-accuracy results:

| Configuration | Accuracy |
|---|---|
| Full pipeline | 78% |
| − re-ranker | 76% |
| − query rewriting | 65% |
| − citation formatting | 78% |

Which component contributes most to accuracy?
options: Re-ranker
Citation formatting
Query rewriting
All contribute equally
questions.why: Removing query rewriting causes the largest drop (13 points), while removing the re-ranker costs 2 points and citation formatting has no measured accuracy effect. Ablations attribute contribution by the drop when a component is removed, not by which component is most complex.

questions.q: Summarizer S1 has ROUGE-L 0.42 and a faithfulness score of 0.71; summarizer S2 has ROUGE-L 0.38 and faithfulness 0.93. For a medical-records use case, which choice is most defensible?
options: S1, because ROUGE-L is the standard summarization metric
Neither, because metrics disagree
S1, because higher lexical overlap implies fewer hallucinations
S2, because factual consistency matters more than a small overlap gain in a high-stakes domain
questions.why: ROUGE rewards wording overlap with a reference but does not penalize fabricated content, so S1 can score higher while hallucinating more. Metric choice should reflect the use case's risks; in medicine, faithfulness dominates.

questions.q: Model A reports 70% on a benchmark in a 5-shot setting and Model B reports 66% zero-shot. What is the correct conclusion?
options: Model A is clearly better
Model B is better because zero-shot is harder
The results are not directly comparable because the evaluation settings differ
Few-shot results are always 4 points higher than zero-shot
questions.why: Number of shots, prompt template and scoring method can shift benchmark results by several points. A fair comparison runs both models under the identical protocol, ideally with the same harness.

questions.q: How does lm-evaluation-harness typically score a multiple-choice task like HellaSwag for a base model?
options: It compares the log-likelihood the model assigns to each candidate answer and picks the highest
It asks the model to generate an essay and grades it with BLEU
It uses a GPT-4 judge for each item
It measures latency on each choice
questions.why: Log-likelihood scoring avoids parsing free-form output, so base models without instruction tuning can be evaluated. Generation-based scoring with answer extraction is used for tasks like GSM8K instead.

questions.q: In lm-evaluation-harness, HellaSwag reports both `acc` and `acc_norm`. What does `acc_norm` correct for?
options: Class imbalance among the answer letters
The bias toward shorter candidates, since longer continuations accumulate lower total log-likelihood
Differences in tokenizer vocabulary size
The number of few-shot examples
questions.why: Summed log-probabilities penalize longer answers simply for having more tokens; `acc_norm` normalizes the score by the continuation's length (in bytes) before choosing. It does not address answer-letter imbalance or tokenizer vocabulary size.

questions.q: On GSM8K, a team samples 16 chain-of-thought solutions per problem and takes the most common final answer. Accuracy rises from 58% to 69%. What is this technique and how should it be reported?
options: Beam search; report as pass@16
Self-consistency (majority voting); report as maj@16 rather than as single-sample accuracy
Ensemble distillation; report as zero-shot accuracy
Contamination; report the original 58% only
questions.why: Self-consistency aggregates multiple reasoning paths and costs 16× the inference compute, so the setting must be stated explicitly. pass@16 would count a problem as solved if any sample is right, which is a looser criterion than majority vote.

questions.q: Why do code evaluations often use greedy decoding for pass@1 but a higher temperature (e.g., 0.8) for pass@100?
options: Higher temperature makes every sample more accurate
Greedy decoding cannot produce runnable code
Diverse samples increase the chance that at least one of many is correct, while greedy is best for a single attempt
pass@100 is defined only for temperature 0.8
questions.why: With 100 attempts, identical greedy outputs would waste the budget; sampling explores different solutions. For a single attempt, the most likely completion typically has the best chance of being correct.

questions.q: An NVIDIA-centric team wants a managed microservice to run academic benchmarks, custom datasets and LLM-as-a-judge evaluations against models served as NIM endpoints. Which component fits?
options: NeMo Curator
TensorRT-LLM
NeMo Guardrails
NeMo Evaluator
questions.why: NeMo Evaluator is the NeMo microservice for evaluating models and pipelines with standard benchmarks, custom data and judge-based metrics. NeMo Curator prepares and filters training data; it does not run evaluations.

questions.q: How can a natural language inference (NLI) model be used to evaluate summary faithfulness?
options: By checking whether each summary sentence is entailed by the source document
By computing perplexity of the summary
By translating the summary and comparing BLEU
By counting named entities in the summary
questions.why: Treating the source as premise and each summary claim as hypothesis, contradictions or neutral (unsupported) predictions flag hallucinations. Low perplexity only shows the text is fluent, not that it is supported.

questions.q: Without access to a reference or retrieval source, a team samples several responses to the same question and checks whether their factual claims agree. Which idea does this follow?
options: BERTScore against a reference
Inconsistency across samples (as in SelfCheckGPT) suggests the model is hallucinating rather than recalling a known fact
Perplexity thresholding on the prompt
ROUGE-L between the question and the answer
questions.why: If a model truly knows a fact, stochastic samples tend to agree; fabricated details vary from sample to sample. BERTScore needs a reference answer, which is unavailable in this setup.

questions.q: A team scores long biographies generated by an LLM by splitting each into short atomic claims and checking what fraction is supported by a knowledge source. Which approach is this?
options: ROUGE-2
MT-Bench
FActScore-style atomic fact precision
Exact match
questions.why: FActScore decomposes long-form text into atomic facts and reports the percentage supported by a source such as Wikipedia, giving a fine-grained factual precision. A single overall true/false judgment would hide partially correct outputs.

questions.q: Which of the following metrics is reference-free, meaning it does not require a gold output?
options: BLEU
ROUGE-L
Exact match
An LLM judge scoring helpfulness against a rubric
questions.why: Rubric-based judging evaluates the output on its own merits (given the input), so no reference answer is required. BLEU, ROUGE and EM all compare the output to one or more references.

questions.q: A team builds an LLM that predicts ticket categories, and future tickets will reflect new products. Which split best estimates production performance?
options: Random split across all dates
Train on older tickets and test on the most recent period
Test on a random 1% of training tickets
Use the same data for training and testing
questions.why: A time-based split simulates deployment, where the model always predicts the future from the past and must cope with drift. Random splits leak future patterns into training and overstate performance.

questions.q: A dataset contains many conversations per customer, and customers have distinctive phrasing. How should the data be split to avoid leakage?
options: Group by customer so each customer appears in only one split
Randomly by conversation turn
Alphabetically by first word
Put all long conversations in the test set
questions.why: Grouped splits stop the model from scoring well by recognizing customer-specific patterns it already saw in training. Random turn-level splits scatter the same customer (and even the same conversation) across splits.

questions.q: After launch, users report failures that the team's golden set never caught. What is the best practice?
options: Freeze the golden set permanently to preserve comparability
Replace the golden set entirely each week
Add triaged production failures as new labeled cases, versioning the set and keeping past results comparable
Remove hard cases so scores stay stable
questions.why: A golden set should grow to cover real failure modes, with explicit versions so scores are compared on the same set version. Freezing it forever lets it drift out of sync with real traffic, and replacing it wholesale destroys comparability.

questions.q: Two models are evaluated on the same 1,000 test questions. Which statistical test is appropriate for comparing their per-item correct/incorrect results?
options: McNemar's test on the discordant pairs
An unpaired two-sample t-test on accuracies
A chi-squared test on vocabulary sizes
Cohen's kappa between the two models
questions.why: Because both models answer the same items, results are paired; McNemar's test focuses on items where exactly one model is correct. An unpaired test ignores this pairing and loses statistical power.

questions.q: How can a team obtain a confidence interval for a corpus-level metric like BLEU whose sampling distribution has no simple formula?
options: Report the metric to more decimal places
Compute the metric on the training set
Use Cohen's kappa
Bootstrap: resample test items with replacement many times and take percentiles of the recomputed metric
questions.why: Bootstrap resampling approximates the sampling variability of any metric empirically. Paired bootstrap (resampling the same items for both systems) is commonly used to test whether one system's BLEU is significantly higher.

questions.q: On a 100-question internal benchmark, model A scores 72% and model B scores 70%. What is the most reasonable interpretation?
options: A is reliably better
B is reliably better
The difference is well within sampling noise; the standard error is about 4–5 points
Both models are contaminated
questions.why: SE ≈ √(0.71·0.29/100) ≈ 0.045, so a 2-point gap is far smaller than the uncertainty. More items (or a paired test) are needed before declaring a winner.

questions.q: A team tunes prompts aggressively against one public leaderboard. Scores rise, but users notice no improvement. Which principle best describes this?
options: Goodhart's law: when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure
Scaling laws
The bias–variance tradeoff
Amdahl's law
questions.why: Optimizing directly for a benchmark exploits its quirks and overfits to it, breaking its link to the capability it was meant to measure. Rotating held-out evals and checking with users counters this.

questions.q: A fine-tuned chat model has slightly higher perplexity on a web-text corpus than its base model but is much better at following instructions. Why is this not a contradiction?
options: Perplexity is calculated incorrectly for chat models
Perplexity measures fit to a text distribution, not usefulness on downstream tasks or alignment with user intent
Instruction-tuned models have a different vocabulary size
Lower perplexity always means worse instruction following
questions.why: Alignment shifts the model's distribution away from raw web text toward helpful responses, which can raise perplexity on generic corpora. Task-specific evaluations and human preferences capture what perplexity cannot; the relationship is not "always" in either direction.

questions.q: Why do BLEU and ROUGE often correlate poorly with human judgments for open-ended chatbot responses?
options: They are too slow to compute on dialogue
They require GPU acceleration
They only work on languages with spaces
Many very different responses can be equally good, so overlap with a single reference is a poor proxy for quality
questions.why: Open-ended tasks have a huge space of valid answers; a good reply phrased differently gets a low score. That is why open-ended assistants are evaluated with human or LLM-judge ratings instead.

questions.q: A creative-writing model produces fluent but repetitive stories. Which metric directly measures lexical diversity of generated outputs?
options: Distinct-n (ratio of unique n-grams to total n-grams)
Exact match
pass@k
Expected Calibration Error
questions.why: Distinct-1 and distinct-2 count how many unique unigrams or bigrams appear relative to the total, so repetitive outputs score low. Self-BLEU between samples is another diversity check, where lower self-BLEU means more diverse outputs.

questions.topic: Confusion matrix for an LLM classifier
questions.q: An LLM routes support requests into Billing, Technical and Account. Overall accuracy is acceptable, but the team suspects Account requests are being misrouted as Billing. What is the most direct way to confirm this?
options: Compute perplexity per class
Compute ROUGE-L between categories
Inspect the confusion matrix of true versus predicted categories
Run an A/B test
questions.why: The confusion matrix's Account-row, Billing-column cell directly counts that specific misroute. Aggregate accuracy hides which classes get confused with which.

questions.topic: Bias of the naive pass@k estimator
questions.q: Instead of the unbiased combinatorial estimator, a team computes pass@k as 1 − (1 − c/n)^k from n samples with c correct. What is the problem with this naive estimator?
options: It overestimates pass@k because it double-counts correct samples
It is unbiased but has higher variance
It cannot be computed when k > 1
It is biased; because 1 − (1 − p)^k is concave in p, plugging in the noisy estimate c/n systematically underestimates pass@k
questions.why: By Jensen's inequality, the expectation of a concave function of a noisy estimate is below the function of the true value. The Codex paper's estimator 1 − C(n−c,k)/C(n,k) computes the exact probability that a random size-k subset of the n samples contains a correct one, which is unbiased.

questions.q: Using the unbiased estimator with n = 10 samples, c = 7 correct and k = 5, what is pass@5 for the problem?
options: Undefined
questions.why: There are only n − c = 3 incorrect samples, so every subset of 5 must contain at least one correct sample; C(3,5) = 0 and pass@5 = 1. Implementations explicitly return 1.0 when n − c < k to avoid computing an invalid binomial coefficient.

questions.q: On a 4,000-byte document, a model's tokenizer produces 1,000 tokens with an average loss of 0.9 nats per token. What is the model's bits per byte (BPB), approximately?
questions.why: Total loss = 1,000 × 0.9 = 900 nats = 900 / ln 2 ≈ 1,298 bits, and 1,298 / 4,000 ≈ 0.32 bits per byte. Dividing nats by bytes without converting to bits gives 0.225, the most common slip; BPB is tokenizer-independent, which is why it is used to compare models with different vocabularies.

questions.q: When computing perplexity of a fixed-context model on documents longer than its context window, why is a sliding window with a stride smaller than the window often used instead of disjoint chunks?
options: Disjoint chunks force tokens at the start of each chunk to be predicted with little context, inflating perplexity
Sliding windows reduce the compute cost
Disjoint chunks double-count tokens
Sliding windows change the tokenizer's vocabulary
questions.why: With overlapping windows, each scored token is conditioned on nearly a full context, giving a value closer to the model's true autoregressive perplexity. The trade-off is more compute, not less, because overlapping regions are re-processed; only non-overlapping target tokens are scored to avoid double-counting.

questions.q:
A developer computes evaluation loss for a padded batch with Hugging Face Transformers:

```python
labels = batch["input_ids"].clone()
out = model(input_ids=batch["input_ids"],
            attention_mask=batch["attention_mask"],
            labels=labels)
ppl = torch.exp(out.loss)
```

Why is this perplexity misleading?
options: `torch.exp` should be replaced by `torch.log`
Causal LMs require labels to be shifted manually by the user
The attention mask causes the loss to ignore all tokens
Pad positions are included in the loss; they should be set to -100 in `labels` so they are ignored
questions.why: The attention mask stops real tokens from attending to padding, but it does not remove pad tokens from the loss — only label value -100 does that. Hugging Face causal LM heads already shift labels internally, so manual shifting would misalign them.

questions.q:
```python
ppls = []
for batch in loader:
    loss = model(**batch).loss          # mean NLL over this batch's tokens
    ppls.append(torch.exp(loss).item())
corpus_ppl = sum(ppls) / len(ppls)
```

What is wrong with `corpus_ppl`?
options: Nothing; averaging per-batch perplexities is equivalent to corpus perplexity
It should take the median instead of the mean
It averages exponentials rather than exponentiating the token-weighted average NLL, which overestimates perplexity and ignores differing token counts
It should multiply the perplexities instead of averaging them
questions.why: Corpus perplexity is exp(Σ token NLL / Σ tokens). Because exp is convex, the mean of per-batch exp(loss) is at least exp of the mean loss, and batches with few tokens get the same weight as large ones.

questions.q: A researcher wants to detect whether specific benchmark items were in a model's pretraining data without access to that data. Which technique fits?
options: Min-k% probability: average the log-probabilities of the lowest-probability k% of tokens; unusually high values suggest memorization
Computing BLEU between the model's answers and the benchmark answers
Measuring time to first token on the items
Running the benchmark with more few-shot examples
questions.why: Unseen text usually contains a few surprising, low-probability tokens, while memorized text has few outliers. This is a membership-inference heuristic and needs calibration against known-unseen text; answer-level BLEU cannot distinguish memorization from genuine ability.

questions.q: A model scores 92% on a public math benchmark but 71% on a version where the same problems are rewritten with new numbers and names. What does this most strongly suggest?
options: The rewritten problems are inherently harder
The model is underfitting
The original benchmark answer key contains errors
Likely contamination or memorization of the original items rather than robust reasoning
questions.why: If difficulty is held constant, a large drop on semantically equivalent variants points to the model having memorized surface forms of the original test items. Perturbed or freshly written variants (as in GSM1K-style studies) are a standard contamination probe.

questions.q: Why did leaderboards like Chatbot Arena move from online Elo updates toward fitting a Bradley–Terry model over all battles?
options: Bradley–Terry requires no human votes

Online Elo results depend on the order in which battles are processed, whereas a maximum-likelihood Bradley–Terry fit over all battles is order-independent and gives more stable estimates with confidence intervals
Bradley–Terry supports only two models
Elo cannot handle ties
questions.why: Online Elo was designed for players whose skill changes over time; static model checkpoints are better served by a joint fit. The ratings remain on an Elo-like scale, and bootstrap gives confidence intervals; Elo can actually handle ties as half-wins.

questions.q: A team finds its fine-tuned model's win rate against a baseline (judged by an LLM) jumped mostly because responses became 2× longer. Which evaluation adjustment addresses this?
options: Report length-controlled win rate, which regresses out the effect of the length difference on judge preference
Increase the max output tokens for the baseline
Switch the judge to temperature 1.0
Truncate both responses to 50 tokens
questions.why: AlpacaEval 2.0's length-controlled win rate fits a model of judge preference with a length term and reports the win rate with that term neutralized, reducing gaming by verbosity. Hard truncation would cut off legitimately complete answers and distort quality.

questions.q: G-Eval-style LLM judging asks the judge to reason with chain-of-thought evaluation steps and then computes the final score as a probability-weighted sum over possible score tokens. What is the main benefit of the probability weighting?
options: It removes the need for a rubric
It makes the judge immune to position bias
It yields finer-grained, less tied scores than taking only the single most likely integer
It converts the judge into a reference-based metric
questions.why: Judges asked for a 1–5 score tend to output the same few integers, producing many ties; weighting by token probabilities gives a continuous expected score that correlates better with humans. It does nothing about position bias, which requires order swapping.

questions.q: An LLM judge frequently approves wrong answers to math questions that it could not solve reliably itself. What mitigation did the MT-Bench authors propose for such categories?
options: Remove math questions from the benchmark
Use a smaller judge model
Ask the judge to rate fluency only
Reference-guided judging: give the judge a correct reference solution to compare against
questions.why: Judges are limited by their own reasoning ability and can be misled by a confident-looking wrong answer; supplying a reference answer markedly reduced grading errors on math. Judging fluency only would hide exactly the errors that matter.

questions.q: Two raters agree on 95% of items, but 94% of all labels are "safe". Their Cohen's kappa is only 0.3. What explains this?
options: Kappa was miscomputed; it can never be below percent agreement by that much
With highly skewed label prevalence, chance agreement p_e is very high, so even high observed agreement leaves little agreement beyond chance
The raters disagreed on most "safe" items
Kappa only applies to ordinal data
questions.why: When nearly everything is "safe", two raters would agree most of the time just by labeling everything safe, so p_e is close to 0.9 and κ = (p_o − p_e)/(1 − p_e) shrinks. Report kappa alongside prevalence and per-class agreement on the rare class.

questions.q: Instead of one large proprietary judge, a team uses a panel of three smaller judges from different model families and aggregates their votes. What is the main motivation?
options: Reducing intra-model bias such as self-preference and lowering variance, often at lower cost
Eliminating the need to validate against humans
Ensuring all three judges give identical scores
Increasing position bias to make results consistent
questions.why: A diverse panel averages out idiosyncratic biases of any one model family, and smaller judges can be cheaper in aggregate. The panel still needs to be checked against human judgments; diversity does not guarantee validity.

questions.q: An A/B test of a new assistant has high variance in "messages per user". Which technique uses each user's pre-experiment behavior to reduce variance and the required sample size?
options: Bonferroni correction
Sequential testing
CUPED (regression adjustment with a pre-period covariate)
Stratified bootstrap of the treatment arm only
questions.why: CUPED subtracts the part of the outcome predicted by a pre-experiment covariate, which is independent of treatment assignment, leaving an unbiased estimate with smaller variance. Bonferroni addresses multiple comparisons and does nothing for variance.

questions.q: Stakeholders insist on monitoring an A/B test continuously and stopping as soon as a result is clear. Which approach keeps the false-positive rate controlled?
options: Use a fixed α = 0.05 at each daily check
Stop only when the p-value drops below 0.05 twice in a row
Double the sample size and peek freely
Use a sequential design, such as alpha-spending boundaries or always-valid p-values (e.g., mSPRT)
questions.why: Sequential methods account for the multiple looks, so the overall Type I error stays at the target level while allowing early stops. Ad-hoc rules like "twice in a row" still inflate the error rate in ways that are not controlled.

questions.q: A team evaluates a new model on 200 benchmark sub-tasks and wants to report which sub-tasks improved without being as conservative as Bonferroni. Which procedure controls the expected proportion of false discoveries?
options: Benjamini–Hochberg
McNemar's test
Cohen's kappa
Holdout validation
questions.why: Benjamini–Hochberg controls the false discovery rate (the expected share of significant findings that are false), giving more power than Bonferroni, which controls the probability of any false positive. McNemar's test could produce the per-sub-task p-values but does not correct for multiplicity.

questions.q: An A/B test randomizes individual chat requests to model A or B and analyzes each request as an independent observation. Heavy users send hundreds of requests. What is the main statistical problem?
options: The test has too few observations
Requests from the same user are correlated, so treating them as independent understates variance and yields overconfident p-values; randomize and analyze at the user level
Request-level randomization guarantees sample ratio mismatch
p-values cannot be computed for chat data
questions.why: The effective sample size is closer to the number of users than the number of requests. Request-level assignment also lets one user see both variants, contaminating experiences; user-level randomization (or clustered standard errors) fixes both.

questions.q: Using the rule of thumb n ≈ 16·p(1−p)/δ² per arm (α = 0.05, 80% power), how many users per arm are needed to detect a change from a 50% to a 55% task-success rate?
options: About 160
About 400
About 1,600
About 6,400
questions.why: n ≈ 16 × 0.25 / 0.05² = 4 / 0.0025 = 1,600 per arm. Forgetting to square δ (16 × 0.25 / 0.05) gives 80, and using δ = 0.025 instead would give 6,400.

questions.q: A fine-tuned LLM classifier is overconfident. The team applies temperature scaling: one scalar T > 1 fitted on a validation set divides all logits. What happens to accuracy?
options: It increases, because predictions become less confident
It decreases, because the logits are smaller
It becomes equal to the ECE
It is unchanged, because dividing logits by a positive constant does not change the argmax
questions.why: Temperature scaling only softens or sharpens the probability distribution, improving calibration metrics like ECE and NLL while leaving predicted labels identical. That is why it is a popular post-hoc fix: no accuracy trade-off.

questions.q: The GPT-4 technical report showed that the pretrained model's multiple-choice confidence was well calibrated. What happened after RLHF-style post-training?
options: Calibration got noticeably worse even though helpfulness improved
Calibration became perfect
Calibration was unchanged
The model stopped outputting probabilities
questions.why: Preference optimization pushes the model toward particular confident answers rather than matching the data distribution, degrading the link between token probabilities and correctness. Teams relying on token probabilities for confidence should re-measure calibration after alignment.

questions.q: A model's predictions fall into two confidence bins: 60 samples with average confidence 0.9 and accuracy 0.7, and 40 samples with average confidence 0.6 and accuracy 0.6. What is the ECE?
questions.why: ECE = (60/100)·|0.9 − 0.7| + (40/100)·|0.6 − 0.6| = 0.6·0.2 + 0 = 0.12. An unweighted average of bin gaps would give 0.10, but ECE weights each bin by its share of samples.

questions.q: A service receives 20 requests per second, and each request takes 3 seconds end to end. In steady state, about how many requests are in flight concurrently?
questions.why: Little's law: concurrency L = arrival rate λ × time in system W = 20 × 3 = 60. Load tests should be configured with realistic concurrency, since latency and throughput measured at concurrency 1 say little about behavior at 60.

questions.q: A model has a time to first token of 0.5 s and an inter-token latency (time per output token) of 20 ms. Approximately how long does a 200-token response take to finish streaming?
questions.why: Total ≈ TTFT + (N − 1) × ITL = 0.5 + 199 × 0.02 ≈ 4.48 s. Dropping TTFT gives 4.0 s; both components matter, and their relative weight depends on prompt length (prefill) versus output length (decode).

questions.q: Which hyperparameter optimization method trains a population of models in parallel and periodically replaces poor performers with copies of good ones whose hyperparameters are then perturbed, producing a schedule rather than a single fixed setting?
options: Grid search
Bayesian optimization with Gaussian processes
Hyperband
Population-based training (PBT)
questions.why: PBT combines exploit (copy weights from better members) and explore (perturb their hyperparameters) during training, effectively learning a hyperparameter schedule. Hyperband also allocates budget adaptively but trains each configuration with fixed hyperparameters and simply stops the weak ones.

questions.q: Optuna's default sampler, TPE, chooses the next hyperparameters by:
options: Evaluating every point on a predefined grid
Modeling densities of good and bad past trials separately and picking candidates that maximize their ratio
Following the gradient of validation loss with respect to the hyperparameters
Sampling uniformly at random with no use of past results
questions.why: TPE splits completed trials into a top quantile and the rest, fits densities l(x) and g(x), and favors candidates with high l(x)/g(x), which corresponds to maximizing expected improvement. It is a sequential model-based (Bayesian) method rather than random or gradient-based search.

questions.q: During LLM pretraining, the loss suddenly spikes and recovers slowly, and it recurs at the same data region. Which response is standard practice?
options: Ignore it, since loss spikes always self-correct
Increase the learning rate to escape the spike faster
Restart from a checkpoint before the spike, skip the offending data batches and/or lower the learning rate
Switch the evaluation metric from loss to BLEU
questions.why: Large-model training reports (e.g., PaLM, OPT) describe rolling back to an earlier checkpoint and skipping problematic batches, sometimes with lower learning rates or tighter gradient clipping. Raising the learning rate typically makes instabilities worse.

questions.q: Tuning hyperparameters directly on a 70B model is prohibitively expensive. Which approach allows tuning on small proxy models and transferring the optimum to the large model?
options: Maximal Update Parametrization (μP), which keeps optimal hyperparameters stable as width grows
Using the same absolute learning rate as a 125M model under standard parametrization
Grid search on the 70B model with one step per trial
Choosing hyperparameters that minimize training loss on the test set
questions.why: Under μP, the optimal learning rate and initialization scale stay approximately constant across model widths ("μTransfer"). Under standard parametrization the optimal learning rate shifts with size, so copying a small model's value directly is unreliable.

questions.q: A capability appears to jump suddenly from near 0% to 60% exact-match accuracy between two model sizes, while per-token log-likelihood on the same task improves smoothly. What does this suggest?
options: The larger model was trained on contaminated data
Exact match is the only valid metric for the task
Log-likelihood is computed incorrectly
