The apparent sharp emergence may partly be an artifact of a discontinuous, all-or-nothing metric
questions.why: Exact match only rewards outputs that are fully correct, so gradual improvements in per-token probability show up as a sudden jump. Continuous metrics reveal smoother scaling, which matters when forecasting capabilities from smaller models.

questions.q: Changing only the answer delimiter and option formatting in an MMLU prompt shifts a model's accuracy by 5 points. What is the most robust evaluation practice?
options: Report the best-scoring format
Evaluate across several prompt templates and report the mean and spread, keeping templates fixed across compared models
Use a different template for each model to match its preferences without disclosure
Remove the answer options
questions.why: LLM benchmark results are sensitive to formatting, so a single template can reflect format luck rather than capability. Reporting the best template per model biases comparisons; varying templates measures robustness explicitly.

questions.q: The same model gets noticeably different MMLU scores from two evaluation frameworks using identical questions. Which difference is the most likely cause?
options: One framework scores only the probability of the answer letter, another the log-likelihood of the full answer text, or one uses free generation with answer extraction
MMLU questions are randomly regenerated per run
One framework uses GPUs and the other CPUs
MMLU has no fixed answer key
questions.why: These scoring choices measure subtly different things and can change rankings, which is why leaderboards specify the harness and settings. Hardware differences cause only tiny numerical variations, not multi-point gaps.

questions.q: An evaluation calls a served model at temperature 0, yet a few outputs differ between runs. What is a likely cause on the serving side?
options: Temperature 0 enables random sampling
The tokenizer is stochastic
Results depend on batch composition: dynamic batching changes kernel choices and floating-point reduction order, which can flip near-tied argmax tokens
The model weights are updated after every request
questions.why: With continuous batching, the same request is computed alongside different neighbors, slightly changing logits; when two tokens are nearly tied, greedy decoding can diverge and the difference propagates. Evaluation reports should acknowledge this residual variance or use batch-invariant kernels where available.

questions.q: A team needs to prove months later exactly which evaluation dataset produced a reported score, even though the file path stayed the same while contents were edited. What practice guarantees this?
options: Recording the file path and modification date in a spreadsheet
Saving only the final score
Keeping the dataset in the same folder forever
Content-addressed versioning (e.g., hashing datasets with tools like DVC or W&B/MLflow artifacts) and logging the hash with each run
questions.why: A content hash changes whenever the data change, so the run record unambiguously identifies the exact bytes evaluated. Paths and timestamps can stay the same, or change, without reflecting content edits.

questions.q: Model B beats model A on both short and long queries when the results are broken down, yet A has the higher overall accuracy. How is this possible?
options: The accuracy was computed incorrectly
The two models were evaluated on different mixes of short and long queries, and the aggregate is dominated by the easier segment
Model B is overfitting
Accuracy cannot be compared across segments
questions.why: This is Simpson's paradox: when segment proportions differ between groups, aggregate comparisons can reverse segment-level ones. Evaluating both models on the identical item set (or reweighting) removes the confound.

questions.q:
A new model's golden-set results:

| Segment | Share | Old | New |
|---|---|---|---|
| General FAQ | 85% | 88% | 92% |
| Refund policy | 10% | 90% | 70% |
| Legal disclaimers | 5% | 95% | 96% |

What is the best decision?
options: Ship, since overall accuracy improved
Reject the model entirely, since one segment regressed
Treat the refund-policy drop as a blocking regression to investigate, since aggregate gains can hide segment failures
Remove the refund segment from the golden set
questions.why: Overall accuracy rises (≈ 88.9% → 90.0%), but a 20-point drop on refund questions could cause real harm. Per-segment thresholds in the regression suite catch this; deleting the segment just hides the problem, and outright rejection ignores that the fix may be targeted.

questions.q: A model scores nearly 100% on single-needle "needle in a haystack" tests up to 128K tokens. Why is this insufficient evidence of strong long-context ability?
options: Needle tests only measure latency
Needle tests require fine-tuning first
Needle tests cannot be run beyond 32K tokens
Retrieving one inserted fact is much easier than multi-hop reasoning, aggregation or tracking many facts across the context, which suites like RULER test
questions.why: Single-needle retrieval often saturates while performance on multi-needle, variable-tracking and aggregation tasks degrades well before the advertised context length. Effective context length should be measured on harder tasks.

questions.q: Which benchmark design best resists contamination for code models over time?
options: Continuously collecting new problems released after each model's training cutoff and evaluating only on those
Reusing HumanEval with renamed function names
Publishing the test set with answers on the web
Increasing the number of few-shot examples
questions.why: "Live" benchmarks such as LiveCodeBench timestamp problems so each model can be scored only on items that did not exist when it was trained. Renaming functions is a shallow perturbation that a model familiar with the original problems can still exploit.

questions.q: In the MT-Bench study, a strong LLM judge agreed with human experts on pairwise preferences about as often as human experts agreed with each other (roughly 80%). How should this be interpreted?
options: The judge is 80% accurate and humans are 100% accurate
The judge can replace all human evaluation for every task
Judge-human agreement near the human-human level suggests the judge is a reasonable proxy for that task setting, but residual biases still need checking
80% agreement means the judge is worse than random
questions.why: Human-human agreement sets a practical ceiling, since human labels are themselves noisy. Matching it supports using the judge in similar settings, but not blanket replacement: domain shift, position/verbosity bias and adversarial outputs can still mislead it.
